title: How Loud Is Too Loud? What the WHO Says About Safe Listening
excerpt: With over a billion young people at risk of noise-induced hearing loss, the World Health Organization's safe listening guidelines offer a practical framework to protect your ears in the age of earbuds.
body:
• The WHO recommends keeping listening volume below 80 decibels — roughly the level of a doorbell — for no more than 40 hours per week to prevent hearing damage.
  • Over 1.1 billion young people aged 12–35 are at risk of hearing loss globally due to unsafe listening with personal audio devices and at entertainment venues.
  • In India, nearly one-third of students using personal listening devices for over four years show signs of high-frequency hearing loss, according to AIIMS Delhi experts.
  • Noise-induced hearing loss is irreversible once it occurs, but entirely preventable through volume control, noise-cancelling headphones, and regular breaks.

The math behind hearing damage is deceptively simple: turn the volume up by 10 decibels, and your safe listening time drops by roughly 75 per cent. At 80 decibels — the sound of a doorbell — the World Health Organization says you can listen safely for 40 hours a week. At 90 decibels, the level of a shouted conversation, that window shrinks to four hours. At 100 decibels, you have just 20 minutes.

This inverse relationship between volume and safety is at the heart of a growing global health crisis. According to WHO data, more than 1.1 billion teenagers and young adults worldwide are at risk of permanent hearing loss due to unsafe listening practices — from earbuds cranked up on public transport to hours spent at concerts, nightclubs and sporting events.

The Science of Sound Damage

Inside the inner ear, thousands of tiny hair cells convert sound vibrations into electrical signals the brain interprets as hearing. Prolonged exposure to loud sound fatigues these cells. Short-term, that produces the muffled hearing or ringing that follows a loud concert. Long-term, the cells die — and unlike most tissue in the body, they do not regenerate.

"A decline in hearing ability caused by prolonged exposure to loud sounds often develops slowly, which is why many people fail to notice it in the early stages," explained Dr Kapil Sikka, Professor of ENT at the All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS) in Delhi. "The damage is irreparable but entirely preventable."

A 2022 review published in BMJ Global Health found that young people commonly listen to personal audio devices at volumes reaching 105 decibels — a level where WHO's safe listening time is just eight minutes per week. At entertainment venues, average sound levels routinely hit 104 to 112 decibels.

India's Growing Hearing Health Challenge

The problem is particularly acute in India, where personal audio device penetration has surged in recent years. The Indian True Wireless Stereo market has expanded rapidly, according to Counterpoint Research, putting high-fidelity sound directly into the ear canals of millions of young Indians.

A survey by the Indian Speech and Hearing Association across Delhi-NCR and Jammu & Kashmir found a communication disorders prevalence rate of over 3 per cent, with hearing impairment rates of 41.2 per cent among those aged 19 to 25. AIIMS Delhi specialists have warned that nearly one-third of students who use personal listening devices for more than four years already show signs of high-frequency hearing loss.

"This is a wake-up call for the 'mobile generation' to stop the indiscriminate usage of headphones, else they would soon have to use hearing aids instead."

— Dr Rajendra Pratap Gupta, public health expert

For diaspora families in the United States, where teens and young adults are similarly immersed in earbud culture, the warning carries added weight. American smartphones can produce up to 115 decibels at maximum volume, according to the American Academy of Otolaryngology.

WHO's Practical Guidelines

The WHO's safe listening framework boils down to a few actionable rules. Keep your device volume at or below 60 per cent of maximum. Use well-fitted, noise-cancelling headphones to reduce the temptation to raise volume in noisy environments. Wear earplugs at concerts and sporting events. Take a 10-minute break for every hour of listening in a loud setting.

Smartphone users can monitor their exposure through built-in health features — Apple's Hearing app in the Control Centre tracks headphone audio levels, while apps like NIOSH-SLM measure ambient sound. The WHO has also developed the hearWHO app for self-screening.

"If you can't hear your parents and your music at the same time, it's too loud," said Dr Shelley Berson, a board-certified otolaryngologist. "If you experience ringing or hearing loss when you take out your earbuds, it's also too loud."

What Comes Next

Health experts say the path forward requires action at multiple levels — from individual listening habits to government regulation of recreational noise limits and manufacturer design standards. WHO recommends that personal audio devices include built-in safe listening features, that entertainment venues use sound limiters, and that schools integrate hearing education into their curricula.

The core message is straightforward: hearing loss from noise exposure is cumulative, irreversible, and — unlike most chronic diseases — almost entirely preventable. The only catch is acting before the damage is done.
